title: Two Sum III - Data structure design
statement:
Build a class `TwoSum` that receives integers one at a time and can tell whether some two of the received integers add up to a given total.

- `TwoSum()` creates the structure with nothing stored.
- `add(number)` stores `number`. The same value may be added more than once, and each copy counts separately.
- `find(value)` returns `true` if two numbers stored by two different `add` calls sum to `value` (they may be equal values when that value was added at least twice), and `false` otherwise.
constraints: At most 10^4 calls in total are made to add and find
notes:
## Intuition

`find(value)` asks the Two Sum question over everything added so far. Keeping a plain list and checking every pair works but costs O(n²) per `find`; storing every pairwise sum makes `find` instant but turns each `add` into O(n) work and O(n²) memory. A middle ground keeps `add` O(1): store how many times each value was added. Then, for each distinct `number`, its partner must be exactly `value - number`, which a hash map checks in O(1).

## Approach

1. Keep a map `counts` from each added value to how many times it was added.
2. `add(number)`: increase `counts[number]` by one.
3. `find(value)`: for each stored `number` with its `count`, compute `complement = value - number`.
4. If `complement` equals `number`, the pair needs two copies, so it works only when `count >= 2`.
5. Otherwise the pair works as soon as `complement` is a key of `counts`.
6. If no stored number has a partner, return `false`.

## Example 1, step by step

After `add(1)`, `add(3)` and `add(5)`, `counts` is `{1: 1, 3: 1, 5: 1}`. `find(4)` starts at `number = 1`: `complement = 3`, which differs from 1 and is stored, so it returns `true`. `find(7)` tries `1` (needs `6`), `3` (needs `4`) and `5` (needs `2`); none is stored, so it returns `false`. Output: `[null, null, null, null, true, false]`.

## Complexity

- Time: `add` is O(1); `find` is O(k), where k is the number of distinct values added.
- Space: O(k) for `counts`.

## Pitfalls

- A single `3` must not answer `find(6)` by pairing with itself; equal partners need `count >= 2`, which is why counts are stored instead of a plain set.
- In Java or C, `value - number` can overflow 32 bits when `value` is near `-2^31`; use a 64-bit type for `complement`.
- `find` on an empty structure, or with only one number, must return `false`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `counts` | map from each added value to how many times it was added |
| `number`, `count` | a stored value and its number of copies |
| `value` | the total that `find` is asked about |
| `complement` | the partner `number` would need, `value - number` |

narration.3: counts remembers each added value and how many copies of it were added.
narration.7: Adding is one map update: bump the count of number by one.
narration.11: Try each distinct stored number as the first half of the pair.
narration.12: The second half would have to be exactly value - number.
narration.13: If the partner is the same value, one stored copy is not enough.
narration.14: It works only if this value was added at least twice.
narration.15: Two copies of number sum to value.
narration.17: A different partner value just has to be stored somewhere.
narration.18: number and complement sum to value.
narration.21: No stored number has a partner, so no pair sums to value.
